title: Can this Rust value cross a thread boundary?
answer: Arc<T> is Send only when T is both Send and Sync

checks.question: Why does rustc refuse thread::spawn(move || x.set(1)) when x is an Arc<Cell<i32>>?
checks.answer: Arc<T> is Send only when T is both Send and Sync, because every clone reaches the same T. Cell<i32> is not Sync, since Cell::set writes through &self with no synchronisation, so Arc<Cell<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync.

checks.question: Which type here is Sync but not Send, and why can’t it move?
checks.answer: MutexGuard<i32>. Dropping it unlocks the mutex, and with POSIX threads a lock must be released on the thread that took it.

checks.question: Is Arc<MutexGuard<i32>> Send?
checks.answer: No. Arc needs T to be both Send and Sync, and MutexGuard<i32> is Sync but not Send, so Arc<MutexGuard<i32>> is neither.

steps.title: rustc refuses to send this Arc to another thread
steps.line: Predict: isn’t Arc the thread-safe pointer? Why is x refused?
steps.caption: x is an Arc, the pointer the standard library provides for sharing one value between threads; here it holds a Cell<i32>. thread::spawn runs a closure on a new thread, and move hands x to that closure. rustc refuses with error E0277, and the error names two traits: Sync, which Cell<i32> lacks, and Send, which Arc<Cell<i32>> needed for the move.
steps.picture: Code, 8 lines. The two traits: 5: = help: the trait `Sync` is not implemented; 6: for `Cell<i32>`; 7: = note: required for `Arc<Cell<i32>>` to; and 1 more.

steps.title: Send and Sync: the two questions in that error
steps.line: Predict: Cell::set writes through a shared &self. Which quadrant holds Cell<i32>?
steps.caption: thread::spawn needs everything its closure owns to be Send: safe to move to another thread. Sync is the other question: can several threads hold a shared reference &T to it at once? The standard library defines T as Sync exactly when &T is Send. The compiler answers both questions for every type, so each type falls in one of four quadrants.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart; 6 labels.

steps.title: Answer: Cell<i32> can move but cannot be shared
steps.line: Predict: now wrap it in Arc. Which quadrant does Arc<Cell<i32>> land in?
steps.caption: Cell::set writes through a shared &self without synchronisation. Two threads sharing &Cell could therefore write to the same value at once, so Cell is not Sync. Moving ownership is different: the old owner gives up the Cell rather than keeping shared access to it. Cell<T> is Send when T is, so a whole Cell<i32> can move to another thread.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Send only” filled; 1 label. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: no” beside Cell<i32>. New in this step: Cell<i32>; Map of the four quadrants, “Send only” filled; 1 label.

steps.title: Answer: Arc<Cell<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync
steps.line: Arc makes its count thread-safe, not the value inside.
steps.caption: Arc<T> is Send only when T is both Send and Sync, and the same holds for Sync. Every clone of an Arc reaches the same T, so a clone moved to another thread shares T between threads, and Arc adds no locking around it. Cell<i32> is Send but not Sync, so Arc<Cell<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync: the point moves from “Send only” to “Neither”, and thread::spawn refuses x.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 3 labels. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside x is Arc<Cell<i32>>. New in this step: x is Arc<Cell<i32>>; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 3 labels.

steps.title: Rc<i32> is neither Send nor Sync, whatever it holds
steps.line: Rc is the single-threaded Arc: its owner count is a plain integer.
steps.caption: Rc is the single-threaded version of Arc: it counts its owners with a plain integer, not an atomic one. Two threads cloning Rcs that share one count could update it at the same moment, which is undefined behaviour. Rc is therefore neither Send nor Sync, whatever it holds. Arc’s atomic count fixes exactly that, and nothing about the value inside.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 2 points; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 1 label. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside Rc<i32>. New in this step: Rc<i32>; Cell<i32>; 1 label.

steps.title: i32 is Send and Sync
steps.line: Predict: three quadrants are filled. What could be Sync but not Send?
steps.caption: Send and Sync are auto traits: the compiler gives them to any type built only from parts that have them. Primitives such as i32 have both, so i32 sits in the top-right quadrant. Each point sits at one fixed spot in its quadrant, so only the quadrant carries meaning.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 3 points; Map of the four quadrants, “Send and Sync” filled; 4 labels. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: yes” beside i32. New in this step: i32; Map of the four quadrants, “Send and Sync” filled; 4 labels.

steps.title: Answer: MutexGuard<i32> can be shared but cannot move
steps.line: Predict: what could make the opening’s Cell safe to share?
steps.caption: Dropping a MutexGuard unlocks its mutex. Rust supports platforms that require the unlocking thread to be the one that took the lock, so the guard cannot move to another thread: it is not Send. A shared &MutexGuard gives access through &i32 without moving the guard, so it is Sync when the value inside is Sync. Send and Sync really are two separate questions: every combination occurs.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 4 points; Map of the four quadrants, “Sync only” filled; 1 label. Note: “Send: no, Sync: yes” beside MutexGuard<i32>. New in this step: MutexGuard<i32>; Map of the four quadrants, “Sync only” filled; 1 label.

steps.title: The fix: Mutex<T> needs only T: Send, and is Sync too
steps.line: Arc clones on several threads reach one T with no added safety.
steps.caption: A Mutex lets one thread at a time use the value inside, behind its lock, so Mutex<T> needs only T: Send, and is then Sync as well: the lock supplies the synchronisation Cell lacks. Arc<T>, as before, needs T to be both. The lines omit ?Sized and the allocator. The setting picks the type built next, from the inside out.
steps.picture: Code, 6 lines; 1 label. This wrapper: 2: unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for Arc<T> {}; 3: unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for Arc<T> {}.

steps.title: Arc<i32> is Send and Sync
steps.line: Arc needs T: Send + Sync; i32 is Send and Sync.
steps.caption: Wrapping i32 in Arc gives Arc<i32>. Arc needs the type inside to be both Send and Sync, and i32 is Send and Sync, so Arc<i32> is Send and Sync. The point stays in “Send and Sync”.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Send and Sync” filled; 2 labels. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: yes” beside x is Arc<i32>.

steps.title: Both thread APIs accept x
steps.line: Here x is Send and Sync: spawn needs Send, scope Sync.
steps.caption: thread::spawn needs a Send closure, and a move closure that owns x is Send only if Arc<i32> is. thread::scope lets threads borrow &x instead, and a closure holding &x is Send only if Arc<i32> is Sync. rustc 1.99.1 accepts both for x: Arc<i32>.

steps.caption: thread::spawn needs everything its closure owns to be Send: safe to move to another thread. Sync is the other question: can several threads hold a shared reference &T to it at once? The standard library defines T as Sync exactly when &T is Send. The compiler answers both questions for every type, so each type falls in one of four quadrants.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart; 6 labels.

steps.title: Answer: Cell<i32> can move but cannot be shared
steps.line: Predict: now wrap it in Arc. Which quadrant does Arc<Cell<i32>> land in?
steps.caption: Cell::set writes through a shared &self without synchronisation. Two threads sharing &Cell could therefore write to the same value at once, so Cell is not Sync. Moving ownership is different: the old owner gives up the Cell rather than keeping shared access to it. Cell<T> is Send when T is, so a whole Cell<i32> can move to another thread.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Send only” filled; 1 label. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: no” beside Cell<i32>. New in this step: Cell<i32>; Map of the four quadrants, “Send only” filled; 1 label.

steps.title: Answer: Arc<Cell<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync
steps.line: Arc makes its count thread-safe, not the value inside.
steps.caption: Arc<T> is Send only when T is both Send and Sync, and the same holds for Sync. Every clone of an Arc reaches the same T, so a clone moved to another thread shares T between threads, and Arc adds no locking around it. Cell<i32> is Send but not Sync, so Arc<Cell<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync: the point moves from “Send only” to “Neither”, and thread::spawn refuses x.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 3 labels. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside x is Arc<Cell<i32>>. New in this step: x is Arc<Cell<i32>>; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 3 labels.

steps.title: Rc<i32> is neither Send nor Sync, whatever it holds
steps.line: Rc is the single-threaded Arc: its owner count is a plain integer.
steps.caption: Rc is the single-threaded version of Arc: it counts its owners with a plain integer, not an atomic one. Two threads cloning Rcs that share one count could update it at the same moment, which is undefined behaviour. Rc is therefore neither Send nor Sync, whatever it holds. Arc’s atomic count fixes exactly that, and nothing about the value inside.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 2 points; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 1 label. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside Rc<i32>. New in this step: Rc<i32>; Cell<i32>; 1 label.

steps.title: i32 is Send and Sync
steps.line: Predict: three quadrants are filled. What could be Sync but not Send?
steps.caption: Send and Sync are auto traits: the compiler gives them to any type built only from parts that have them. Primitives such as i32 have both, so i32 sits in the top-right quadrant. Each point sits at one fixed spot in its quadrant, so only the quadrant carries meaning.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 3 points; Map of the four quadrants, “Send and Sync” filled; 4 labels. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: yes” beside i32. New in this step: i32; Map of the four quadrants, “Send and Sync” filled; 4 labels.

steps.title: Answer: MutexGuard<i32> can be shared but cannot move
steps.line: Predict: what could make the opening’s Cell safe to share?
steps.caption: Dropping a MutexGuard unlocks its mutex. Rust supports platforms that require the unlocking thread to be the one that took the lock, so the guard cannot move to another thread: it is not Send. A shared &MutexGuard gives access through &i32 without moving the guard, so it is Sync when the value inside is Sync. Send and Sync really are two separate questions: every combination occurs.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 4 points; Map of the four quadrants, “Sync only” filled; 1 label. Note: “Send: no, Sync: yes” beside MutexGuard<i32>. New in this step: MutexGuard<i32>; Map of the four quadrants, “Sync only” filled; 1 label.

steps.title: The fix: Mutex<T> needs only T: Send, and is Sync too
steps.line: One thread at a time holds the lock, so T need not be Sync.
steps.caption: A Mutex lets one thread at a time use the value inside, behind its lock, so Mutex<T> needs only T: Send, and is then Sync as well: the lock supplies the synchronisation Cell lacks. Arc<T>, as before, needs T to be both. The lines omit ?Sized and the allocator. The setting picks the type built next, from the inside out.
steps.picture: Code, 6 lines; 1 label. This wrapper: 5: unsafe impl<T: Send> Send for Mutex<T> {}; 6: unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for Mutex<T> {}.

steps.title: Mutex<Cell<i32>> is Send and Sync
steps.line: Mutex needs T: Send; Cell<i32> is Send but not Sync.
steps.caption: Wrapping Cell<i32> in Mutex gives Mutex<Cell<i32>>. Mutex needs the type inside to be Send, and Cell<i32> is Send but not Sync, so Mutex<Cell<i32>> is Send and Sync. The lock lets one thread at a time reach the value, so Mutex adds Sync. The point moves from “Send only” to “Send and Sync”.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Send and Sync” filled; 2 labels. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: yes” beside x is Mutex<Cell<i32>>.

steps.title: Both thread APIs accept x
steps.line: Here x is Send and Sync: spawn needs Send, scope Sync.
steps.caption: thread::spawn needs a Send closure, and a move closure that owns x is Send only if Mutex<Cell<i32>> is. thread::scope lets threads borrow &x instead, and a closure holding &x is Send only if Mutex<Cell<i32>> is Sync. rustc 1.99.1 accepts both for x: Mutex<Cell<i32>>. The opening’s Cell can cross once a Mutex guards it.

steps.title: rustc refuses to send this Arc to another thread
steps.line: Predict: isn’t Arc the thread-safe pointer? Why is x refused?

steps.picture: Code, 8 lines. The two traits: 5: = help: the trait `Sync` is not implemented; 6: for `Cell<i32>`; 7: = note: required for `Arc<Cell<i32>>` to; and 1 more.

steps.title: Send and Sync: the two questions in that error
steps.line: Predict: Cell::set writes through a shared &self. Which quadrant holds Cell<i32>?
steps.caption: thread::spawn needs everything its closure owns to be Send: safe to move to another thread. Sync is the other question: can several threads hold a shared reference &T to it at once? The standard library defines T as Sync exactly when &T is Send. The compiler answers both questions for every type, so each type falls in one of four quadrants.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart; 6 labels.

steps.title: Answer: Cell<i32> can move but cannot be shared
steps.line: Predict: now wrap it in Arc. Which quadrant does Arc<Cell<i32>> land in?
steps.caption: Cell::set writes through a shared &self without synchronisation. Two threads sharing &Cell could therefore write to the same value at once, so Cell is not Sync. Moving ownership is different: the old owner gives up the Cell rather than keeping shared access to it. Cell<T> is Send when T is, so a whole Cell<i32> can move to another thread.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Send only” filled; 1 label. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: no” beside Cell<i32>. New in this step: Cell<i32>; Map of the four quadrants, “Send only” filled; 1 label.

steps.title: Answer: Arc<Cell<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync
steps.line: Arc makes its count thread-safe, not the value inside.
steps.caption: Arc<T> is Send only when T is both Send and Sync, and the same holds for Sync. Every clone of an Arc reaches the same T, so a clone moved to another thread shares T between threads, and Arc adds no locking around it. Cell<i32> is Send but not Sync, so Arc<Cell<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync: the point moves from “Send only” to “Neither”, and thread::spawn refuses x.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 3 labels. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside x is Arc<Cell<i32>>. New in this step: x is Arc<Cell<i32>>; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 3 labels.

steps.title: Rc<i32> is neither Send nor Sync, whatever it holds
steps.line: Rc is the single-threaded Arc: its owner count is a plain integer.
steps.caption: Rc is the single-threaded version of Arc: it counts its owners with a plain integer, not an atomic one. Two threads cloning Rcs that share one count could update it at the same moment, which is undefined behaviour. Rc is therefore neither Send nor Sync, whatever it holds. Arc’s atomic count fixes exactly that, and nothing about the value inside.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 2 points; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 1 label. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside Rc<i32>. New in this step: Rc<i32>; Cell<i32>; 1 label.

steps.title: i32 is Send and Sync
steps.line: Predict: three quadrants are filled. What could be Sync but not Send?
steps.caption: Send and Sync are auto traits: the compiler gives them to any type built only from parts that have them. Primitives such as i32 have both, so i32 sits in the top-right quadrant. Each point sits at one fixed spot in its quadrant, so only the quadrant carries meaning.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 3 points; Map of the four quadrants, “Send and Sync” filled; 4 labels. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: yes” beside i32. New in this step: i32; Map of the four quadrants, “Send and Sync” filled; 4 labels.

steps.title: Answer: MutexGuard<i32> can be shared but cannot move
steps.line: Predict: what could make the opening’s Cell safe to share?
steps.caption: Dropping a MutexGuard unlocks its mutex. Rust supports platforms that require the unlocking thread to be the one that took the lock, so the guard cannot move to another thread: it is not Send. A shared &MutexGuard gives access through &i32 without moving the guard, so it is Sync when the value inside is Sync. Send and Sync really are two separate questions: every combination occurs.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 4 points; Map of the four quadrants, “Sync only” filled; 1 label. Note: “Send: no, Sync: yes” beside MutexGuard<i32>. New in this step: MutexGuard<i32>; Map of the four quadrants, “Sync only” filled; 1 label.

steps.title: The fix: Mutex<T> needs only T: Send, and is Sync too
steps.line: With T: Send, Mutex<T> is Send and Sync, as Arc needs.
steps.caption: A Mutex lets one thread at a time use the value inside, behind its lock, so Mutex<T> needs only T: Send, and is then Sync as well: the lock supplies the synchronisation Cell lacks. Arc<T>, as before, needs T to be both. The lines omit ?Sized and the allocator. The setting picks the type built next, from the inside out.
steps.picture: Code, 6 lines; 1 label. Both wrappers: 2: unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for Arc<T> {}; 3: unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for Arc<T> {}; 4: // std/src/sync/poison/mutex.rs:238, 257; and 2 more.

steps.title: Mutex<Rc<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync
steps.line: Mutex needs T: Send; Rc<i32> is neither Send nor Sync.
steps.caption: Wrapping Rc<i32> in Mutex gives Mutex<Rc<i32>>. Mutex needs the type inside to be Send, and Rc<i32> is neither Send nor Sync, so Mutex<Rc<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync. The point stays in “Neither”.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 2 labels. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside x is Mutex<Rc<i32>>.

steps.title: Arc<Mutex<Rc<i32>>> is neither Send nor Sync
steps.line: Arc needs T: Send + Sync; Mutex<Rc<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync.
steps.caption: Wrapping Mutex<Rc<i32>> in Arc gives Arc<Mutex<Rc<i32>>>. Arc needs the type inside to be both Send and Sync, and Mutex<Rc<i32>> is neither Send nor Sync, so Arc<Mutex<Rc<i32>>> is neither Send nor Sync. The point stays in “Neither”.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled; 2 labels. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside x is Arc<Mutex<Rc<i32>>>. New in this step: x is Arc<Mutex<Rc<i32>>>; 2 labels.

steps.title: Neither thread API accepts x
steps.line: Here x is neither Send nor Sync: spawn needs Send, scope Sync.
steps.caption: thread::spawn needs a Send closure, and a move closure that owns x is Send only if Arc<Mutex<Rc<i32>>> is. thread::scope lets threads borrow &x instead, and a closure holding &x is Send only if Arc<Mutex<Rc<i32>>> is Sync. rustc 1.99.1 rejects both for x: Arc<Mutex<Rc<i32>>>.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; “Compiles?”, 2 labelled values; Map of the four quadrants, “Neither” filled. Rejected: x is Arc<Mutex<Rc<i32>>>. New in this step: “Compiles?”, 2 labelled values.
